source.title: Data-Efficient Scaling-Law Discovery for Recommendation Systems via Coupled Hyperparameter Scaling
source.authors: John Martabano Landy; Louis C. Tiao; Yao Xuan; Luc Kien Hang; Rupinder P. Khandpur; Arvind M. Vepa; Srinidhi Raghavendran; Anirudh Agrawal; Xiaoyi Leo Liu; Jiang Liu; Peggy Yao; Alireza Vahdatpour; Djordje Gligorijevic

record.tranche_reason: It evaluates scaling relationships in recommendation and ads ranking models, a setting beyond language-model pretraining. Its most direct result for the claim is a figure comparing an inverse-power frontier fit with observed recommendation-model results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports recommendation-model quality and cost frontiers, but most of its architecture-search, deployment, and training-parameter results do not test the specified language-model claims. Appendix C.5 is the relevant result: it fits an inverse-power curve to six initialization frontier points and compares the curve with later observed results in Figure 10. The comparison is shown only in a figure. Cited results and discussion of language-model scaling laws are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study uses power-law-shaped (scaling-informed) surrogates as a tool for architecture search in recommendation models. It reports only that method's search and deployment performance. Its one explicit power-law fit (App. C.5) is NE against inference FLOPs across architectures within one search space (about 20–160 MFLOPs, not orders of magnitude). That fit is shown only in a figure, with no accuracy measure. None of this measures loss scaling in parameters, data or training compute in another regime.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors present the scaling layer plus Axia as an automated, uncertainty-aware way to learn model-specific complexity–quality frontiers and allocate serving compute. They report a 0.66% mean offline NE gain and 0.36% cumulative online lift over 34 models. They also assert that ranking models show predictable, broadly power-law scaling, but give no quantified fit supporting this. They draw no conclusion on how well the inverse-power fit predicts the frontier.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns recommendation-model architecture and inference-cost frontiers, using an inverse-power curve and Gaussian-process surrogates; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that attainable frontiers vary with scaling-layer grouping and rules; at a fixed number of coordinates, different interaction-width rules can yield different frontiers.

fits_no_version.finding: In one recommendation model, an inverse-power curve NE(F)=a+b/F^c is fitted to six initialization frontier points (NE vs inference FLOPs). It is compared graphically with the observed 20-run frontier, with no error metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The best-attainable quality vs inference-cost frontier across architectures of a ranking model follows an inverse power law.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed number of scaling coordinates (k=3), different interaction-width grouping/rule variants give materially different attainable NE–FLOPs frontiers under a 20-run budget (Figs 3–4). Hypervolume rises from 1 to 3 coordinates and falls at 6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation models, how architectural capacity axes are coupled and scaled changes the attainable quality–cost frontier.

record.problems: The directly relevant curve comparison is presented only in Figure 10, without a textual assessment or numerical prediction-error measure. Absolute quality values are confidential. Controlled scaling-layer comparisons are demonstrated on a single representative model.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted as rows because they concern candidate-search performance, recommendation-model deployments, training-parameter tuning, or cited studies rather than the power-law form tested here.

untested.parts: All; no language-model pretraining loss scaling.
All; no extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger.
All; no language-model shape study at fixed parameter count.
No scaling of recommendation-model loss with parameters, data or training compute over orders of magnitude; no image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.
All; no comparison of fitted exponents across fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests classification is downgraded: the power-law form is used as a surrogate prior, and the only fit is an architecture frontier against inference FLOPs over a narrow range, shown only in a figure. Most results are method-vs-baseline comparisons and production deployment gains. Appendix A notes that fitted exponents are not comparable to language-model studies.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or training compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends in language-model training.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count in language models.
The paper concerns recommendation models, not image or video models; it does not test repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer as instances of the same power-law form.
Downstream-task predictability from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation on the stated fitting choices, and systematic curve bending.

rows.subject: production parameterization (model name not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Fit an inverse-power curve to initialization frontier points and compare its predicted frontier with later observed results.

conditions.value: empirical frontier from 16 initialization and four adaptive observations

rows.measure: Inverse-power frontier prediction compared with the observed complexity–quality frontier
rows.note: The text identifies the fitted curve as NE(F) = a + b/F^c, but does not state its predictive accuracy or describe how closely it matches the later observed frontier.
rows.check: The fit is NE against inference FLOPs over architecture configurations at fixed training data, spanning under one order of magnitude. It is not a training-scaling power law, so it does not bear on V5. No prediction-error number is given; the comparison is figure only.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
